reason: The narrative culminates in the salvation and deliverance of the Hebrew people from Haman's plot to destroy them. Through a series of providential events—Esther's rise to queenship, the revelation of the assassination plot, and the reversal of the genocide decree—the Jewish people are saved and establish the festival of Purim to commemorate their deliverance. Though God (Yahweh) is never explicitly named in this text (making it unique among biblical books), the narrative arc demonstrates the preservation of the Hebrew people as a central outcome. This preservation can reasonably be interpreted as reflecting divine purposes, particularly given Mordecai's reference to help coming to the Jews 'from another place' (4:14), which many scholars understand as an implicit reference to divine intervention.
